newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan stocks end sharply lower on Formosa worry.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan stocks end sharply lower on Formosa worry.

text.p: Taiwan share prices ended lower on Monday on bearish sentiment triggered by controversy over a Formosa Plastics China investment and U.S. disciplinary actions against a Taiwan bank, brokers said.

The benchmark index, hit by big declines in plastics and financial shares, slumped more than two percent in late trade but recovered slightly to close 115.5 points or 1.42 percent lower at 8,004.2. Turnover was an active T$126.7 billion.
Plastic shares, particularly the four Formosa Plastics group members, fell 2.52 percent while financial issues tumbled 2.5 percent.

"Worries of possible government disciplinary actions against Formosa group dragged down the index, which at one point plunged 2.13 percent to 7,847 points," said analyst Oliver Fang of National Securities.
Bargain hunting by institutional investors on major shares helped the index claw back to the 8,000-point level.

Brokers said the downward trend reflected the psychological impact of a government vow to punish Formosa if it were found to have sent money illegally to China to fund its US$3 billion thermal power plant project in coastal Zhangzhou city.

Group chairman Wang Yung-ching's confirmation on Saturday that the project had begun without Taiwan's authorisation angered Taipei, which vowed to find out how it financed what would be biggest Taiwan-funded China investment to date.
Officials launched an inquiry into Formosa violated Taiwan law by financing the China project without Taipei's approval.

Four Formosa group members fell, though brokers said late bargain-hunting helped stave off further damage for the heavily weighted Formosa Plastics, which fell T$1 to T$69.5, and ally Nan Ya Plastics, which dropped T$2 to T$62.
Formosa Chemical Fibre dropped T$1.8 or 4.36 percent to T$39.5, and Formosa Taffeta fell T$1.8 or 5.25 percent to T$32.5.

Financial shares turned bearish after the U.S. Federal Reserve imposed a US$5 million fine on Taiwan's International Commercial Bank of China for allegedly filing inaccurate reports during its aquisition of Chinese American Bank in the 1980s.
Brokers cited concerns that the U.S. move could affect fund operation of the bank, which has used Chinese American Bank to finance Taiwan's purchases of U.S. weapons.
A trading range of 7,800 -8,000 was seen for Tuesday.

The over-the-counter index on Monday closed up at 3.74 points, or 1.36 percent at 279.49, as investors -- fearing further losses at the main exchange -- shifted some investments into the fledgling OTC market, brokers said.
